sentences.text: Revenue, net interest income plus noninterest income, rose from $96.6 billion in FY2016 to $182 billion in FY2025, a 7.3% CAGR [D5][D206].
The path was a step change rather than a smooth compound: revenue was $120 billion in FY2020, $129 billion in FY2022 and $158 billion in FY2023 [D86][D134][D159].
The FY2023 jump of 22.9% came as net interest income rose 33.8%, with higher rates lifting net interest income [D179][D174][P36].
FY2025 growth slowed to 2.8% as net interest income grew 3.1% and noninterest income 2.4% [D226][D221][D222].
North America supplied 76.6% of FY2025 revenue but only 0.2pp of its growth, while Asia-Pacific added 1.2pp on 17.3% growth [D249][D251][D301][D300].
Net interest income of $95.4 billion rose 3% on higher Markets net interest income and higher Card Services revolving balances, largely offset by deposit margin compression [F10][P28].
Noninterest revenue of $87.0 billion rose 2%, held back by the absence of the $7.9 billion Visa gain recorded in FY2024 [F20][P27].
Operating costs grew 1.4pp faster than revenue, at 4.2% against 2.8% [D225][D226].
Diluted EPS grew 13.9% a year against net income's 9.7%, helped by a 3.4% cut in the diluted share count in FY2025 [F115][F113][D224].
The efficiency ratio was 52.4% in FY2025 against a 57.2% window median and a 51.7% window low in FY2024 [D207][D333][D331].
Noninterest expense of $95.6 billion rose 4%, driven by higher compensation, brokerage and distribution fees, and technology and marketing investment [X137][P26].
The credit-loss provision was 7.8% of revenue in FY2025 against a 6.0% peer median, the 75th percentile of four peers [D208][D341][D340].
In FY2025 net margin of 31.2% sat 21.1pp below the 52.3% net interest income share of revenue [D210][D209].
Operating cash flow is not a meaningful earnings-quality measure for a bank; FY2025 operating cash flow was -$148 billion against net income of $57.0 billion [F60][F30].
The outflow came from higher trading assets, higher securities borrowed, net loan originations and higher other assets [P21].
Capital return was $48.2 billion in FY2025, $31.6 billion of buybacks and $16.6 billion of dividends, against $57.0 billion of net income [D205][X102][X112][F30].
Return on average equity was 16.1% in FY2025, the 100th percentile of seven bank peers against an 11.8% median [D213][D338][D339].
Loans were 57.3% of deposits, up from 43.1% in FY2021 as deposits outgrew lending [D211][D115].
Loans rose $121.1 billion, driven by higher CIB Markets loans and securities-based lending in AWM on higher client demand [P4].
Shareholders' equity grew 4.0% a year over the window while buybacks and dividends reached $48.2 billion in FY2025 [F119][D205].
FY2021 to FY2025 net income in the table comes from the proxy's pay-versus-performance table, not the 10-K, and differs by up to 0.10% [R1][F26][X16][F30][X20].
The gap is immaterial to every ratio here, but the 10-K figures should be used where precision matters [R1].
FY2020 pretax income and income tax were later restated to $35.8 billion and $6.7 billion from $35.4 billion and $6.3 billion first reported [R2][R3][X63][X73].
The FY2020 tax rate and net margin comparisons carry that recast and should not anchor a conclusion [R2][R3].
If the efficiency ratio moves above the 57.2% window median from 52.4% in FY2025, the cost trend has reversed; it appears in the FY2026 10-K [D207][D333].
If the credit-loss provision rises above 7.8% of revenue in FY2025, credit costs are still climbing; it appears in the FY2026 10-K [D208].
If net interest income growth falls below the FY2025 3.1%, deposit margin compression is outweighing balance-sheet growth; it appears in the FY2026 10-K [D221].
